title: Secularism
notes: Cited for: the First Amendment's religion clauses; France's 1905 law and laicite as a private-religion, secular public sphere; India adding 'secular' to its preamble in 1976, Gandhi's and Nehru's ideals, religious personal law; Holyoake first using 'secularism' in 1851.

title: The Law of 1905
notes: Cited for: Article 1 (the Republic ensures freedom of conscience) and Article 2 (neither acknowledges, pays for nor subsidises any form of worship) of France's 1905 separation law.

title: Atheism
notes: Cited for: atheism as the critique and denial of metaphysical beliefs in God or spiritual beings; Greek atheos, 'godless'; agnosticism leaves the question open.

title: Agnosticism
notes: Cited for: T. H. Huxley introducing 'agnosticism' in 1869 at the Metaphysical Society; his contrast with the 'Gnostic' of Church history; agnostics hold they do not know whether God exists.

title: Humanism: FAQs
notes: Cited for (attributed, as the movement's own description): the Minimum Statement on Humanism; many humanists are atheists, others agnostic; humanists do not believe in gods or an afterlife.

title: Religious 'Nones' in America: Who They Are and What They Believe
notes: Cited for: among US nones, 17% atheist, 20% agnostic, 63% 'nothing in particular'; most believe in God or another higher power; about half spiritual; two-thirds question religious teachings, 47% dislike religious organizations (survey July 31 to Aug. 6, 2023).

title: Decline of Christianity in the U.S. Has Slowed, May Have Leveled Off (2023-24 Religious Landscape Study)
notes: Cited for: US adults 62% Christian, 29% unaffiliated; unaffiliated 16% in 2007, 23% in 2014; 36,908 respondents; the unaffiliated share has plateaued; 22% of adults raised Christian no longer identify as Christian.

title: Peter L. Berger and the Sociology of Religion (Titus Hjelm, UCL Discovery archive version)
notes: Cited for: Berger's 1967 definition of secularization in The Sacred Canopy; the early Berger's view of secularization as an inevitable result of modernization; his 1999 reversal ('as furiously religious as it ever was'); agreement that structural secularization happened in much of Europe.

title: Secularization: In Defence of an Unfashionable Theory (Steve Bruce)
notes: Cited for: Steve Bruce's 2011 defence of secularization theory, tying religion's decline in power, popularity and prestige to modernization.

title: The Myth of Religious Violence: Secular Ideology and the Roots of Modern Conflict (William T. Cavanaugh)
notes: Cited for: Cavanaugh's 2009 argument that there is no transhistorical, transcultural essence of religion, that what counts as religious or secular depends on configurations of power, and that religion as especially violence-prone is a legitimating myth of Western society.

title: Cosmic war on a global scale: An interview with Mark Juergensmeyer (The Immanent Frame, 2010)
publisher: Social Science Research Council (The Immanent Frame)
notes: Cited for: Juergensmeyer's definition of 'cosmic war'; his view that violence has social, political and economic causes and that religion supplies a structure of justification and meaning.

title: Terror in the Mind of God, Fourth Edition (Mark Juergensmeyer)
notes: Cited for: the book's study, drawing on interviews, of violence among Christian, Muslim, Jewish, Hindu, Sikh and Buddhist groups.

title: The Varieties of Religious Experience (William James, 1902)
notes: Cited for: James's four marks of mystical states (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity), the first two sufficient; 'hardly altered by differences of clime or creed'; 'the supposed unanimity largely disappears'.

title: Sufism
notes: Cited for: Sufism as mystical Islamic belief and practice seeking divine love and knowledge through direct personal experience of God.

title: Kabbala
notes: Cited for: Kabbalah as esoteric Jewish mysticism; the Zohar ('Book of Splendour') from medieval Spain, in some circles given a sanctity rivaling the Torah.

title: Saint Teresa of Ávila
notes: Cited for: Teresa of Ávila (born 1515), Spanish Carmelite nun and mystic; The Interior Castle, published 1588; first woman named a doctor of the church, 1970.

title: Zen
notes: Cited for: Zen as a school of East Asian Buddhism named from Sanskrit dhyana, 'meditation'; awakening through meditation, 'a special transmission outside the scriptures'.

title: Mysticism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
notes: Cited for: perennialism (Huxley 1945) and the common-core view; Steven Katz's 1978 constructivism, that a mystic's milieu over-determines mystical experience.

title: The not-so-new religious movements: changes in 'the cult scene' over the past forty years (Eileen Barker, Temenos, 2014)
publisher: London School of Economics (LSE Research Online)
notes: Cited for: all religions were new at inception; church, sect, denomination and cult as once non-judgmental terms; the negative overtones of 'cult'; definition versus discovery; scholars preferring NRM since the 1970s; no generalizing about NRMs; judge each by what it believes and does; Inform founded 1988.

title: New religious movement
notes: Cited for: 'new religious movement' as the generally accepted term for what is sometimes, often pejoratively, called a cult; the brainwashing concept peaked in the 1970s and has lost credibility.

title: Commemorating 130 Years of the Parliament of the World's Religions
notes: Cited for: the Parliament convened 11 to 27 September 1893 in the Memorial Art Palace (later the Art Institute of Chicago); regarded as the origin of the modern interfaith movement; Native Americans excluded.

title: World Parliament of Religions, 1893 (Boston Collaborative Encyclopedia of Western Theology)
notes: Cited for: English-speaking Christian representatives delivered 152 of 194 papers at the 1893 Parliament.

title: Vivekananda
notes: Cited for: Vivekananda's final address at the 1893 Parliament: every religion's banner will soon read 'Help and not fight'.

title: Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions: Nostra Aetate
notes: Cited for (attributed, as the Church's own teaching): proclaimed by Pope Paul VI on 28 October 1965; 'rejects nothing that is true and holy'; esteem for Muslims; decries antisemitism; 'ever must proclaim Christ'; dialogue and collaboration.

title: Dialogue Principles (Leonard Swidler's Dialogue Decalogue)
notes: Cited for: Swidler's rules: the essential purpose of dialogue is to learn; each participant describes their own faith; compare ideals with ideals and practice with practice.

title: Allah
notes: Cited for: Allah is the standard Arabic word for God, used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews as well as Muslims; probably a contraction of al-Ilah, 'the God'.
